summary: Documents the interface for the IBM 5250 Telnet implementation, which lets 5250-style terminals be used over TCP/IP. It is informational and describes an existing implementation, not a standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1205 explains how a Telnet client can act like an IBM 5250 work station. It describes the options to negotiate and the header placed before each record.

subtitle: How Telnet carries the IBM 5250 work-station data stream between a client and server.

tldr.problem: Hosts needed a description of the interface used by IBM's 5250 Telnet implementation so a client could emulate a 5250 work station.
tldr.mechanism: The client and server agree on Telnet binary, end-of-record, and terminal-type options, then exchange records containing a 5250 header and data stream.
tldr.outcome: This is informational documentation, not a standard. RFC 1205 has been updated by RFC 2877.

today: RFC 1205 is an Informational document and has been updated by RFC 2877.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 1205 documents the interface to IBM's 5250 Telnet implementation. It is intended to help someone implement a Telnet client that emulates an IBM 5250 work station.

The memo does not describe every 5250 command or aid code. It points to IBM's Functions Reference Manual for those details and includes corrections and additions to that manual. The RFC explicitly says it does not specify a standard.
sections.plainLanguage: This document helps a programmer make a Telnet client behave like a particular IBM terminal. It does not define a general Telnet standard or describe every terminal command.

sections.title: Agreeing on Telnet Options
sections.content:
RFC 1205 defines no new Telnet options for 5250 mode. The client and server must agree to use Binary, End-Of-Record (EOR), and Terminal-Type. The terminal-type option lets the client name the model it emulates.

The example negotiation has the server request the terminal type, and the client replies with its type. They then negotiate EOR and binary transmission in both directions. These agreements let the peers exchange 5250 records in the expected form.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending 5250 data, the client and server agree on how to send bytes and mark record endings. The client also tells the server which terminal model it represents.

sections.title: The 5250 Record Header
sections.content:
The data stream contains a header followed by the 5250 work-station data. The fixed header is 6 octets. It contains the logical record length, a record type that should be 12A0 hex for General Data Stream, and a reserved field.

A variable part follows. It is currently 4 octets: one octet gives its length, a 16-bit flags field reports conditions such as an attention key, and an 8-bit opcode identifies the requested operation. The record ends with IAC EOR. Some operations contain only a header and this ending marker.
sections.plainLanguage: Each record starts with a small header that gives its length, kind, status flags, and operation. The 5250 data follows, then Telnet's end-of-record marker.

sections.title: Examples of Record Exchanges
sections.content:
The RFC gives record-flow examples for a device query, cancelling an invitation to send user data, and a System Request operation. A server can query the client's capabilities, and the client returns a Query Reply describing the display and controller.

For System Request, the client signals the request. The server cancels the current invitation, saves the screen, presents a menu, and later restores the saved screen and invites the work station again. The examples show the order of records; implementations may differ in internal details.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show which side sends each record and what happens next. In a System Request, the server pauses normal work, handles the request, then restores the screen and resumes.

sections.title: Corrections and Data-Stream Additions
sections.content:
Section 5 acts as an addendum to the referenced IBM manual. It corrects the Insert Cursor order value and describes changes to cursor handling, transparent fields, and input commands.

It also adds a Move Cursor order, a Transparent Data order, and a Query command with a reply describing device capabilities. These notes supplement the manual; they do not replace its complete description of the 5250 data stream.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo corrects a value in IBM's manual and describes several additions. These include commands to move the cursor, send unformatted data, and ask a display what it supports.
